utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution, and our next witness is ST-113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in by the Usher, we understand, Mr. Hannis, the Prosecution is seeking -- is expecting to lead him for an hour as a 92 ter witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did ask for that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you enlighten us as to why?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in his prior testimony in the Krajisnik case obviously the primarily focus was on his relationships with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. For this case, because we are focusing on the police aspects of the case, I think I need to elaborate on some of his testimony and some of the documents relating to the war commissions as they relate to the war staff; his meeting in the Zvornik; and dealings with information he received about the problems with the police and the paramilitaries, et cetera. I'm pretty sure I will finish before the end of our regular time today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Should you not have called him as a viva voce then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have a time-limit and a number of witnesses, and we thought this was the best combination. I will just tell you my personal experience in the Milutinovic case was we called a number of witnesses as what I called "combo" witnesses, with a nod to McDonald's, I guess, in that they were both 92 ter and viva. Because often times they have given statements that, to recreate in viva voce in this case might take days, whereas I wanted that, but I also wanted the unique aspect that contained to this particular case or in the MOS case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. Would you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dragan Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 20th of April, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your occupation, your profession, is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an MD, a doctor, a pediatrician. That's my specialisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb. And an Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have given testimony before in other cases before this Tribunal, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you are familiar with the procedure that we follow which is pretty well standard in terms of courtrooms, that is, that the side calling you, in this case the Prosecution, would first ask you questions, after which the lawyers representing each of the two accused would have a period to ask you questions in cross-examination. Then you would be returned to -- the Prosecution would then have a right to re-examine you, and the Chamber may have questions of you. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, or doctor, you previously testified in the Krajisnik case before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to coming to court today, did you have a chance to review your testimony from that trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having done that, were you satisfied that the record as recorded accurately reflected your testimony and that if you were asked the same questions today, you would give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything was recorded accurately, and I would provide identical answers today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would tender his prior transcripts. I think they've given four separate numbers for the four separate days, as well as the associated documents in the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document in the 92 ter package shall be admitted as P00397, the specific numbers will be communicated to everyone in due course. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Just briefly, I understand that you were an athlete of some standing in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was a gymnast, and I was in the youth administration of Yugoslavia and the senior administration of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you became involved in politics in what year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Toward the end of 1989.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I was a member of the youth team and the senior team of the former Yugoslavia, team of gymnasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thanks for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You formed a political party in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1990, I began preparations to establish a political party, and I formed the party in -- on the 2nd or 3rd of May in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where you were living and working in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, I was living in Sarajevo, and I was completing my specialisation in pediatrics at the pediatrics clinic in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you a document, the 65 ter number 10151. This will be up on the screen in a moment, Doctor. And I will tell you, it purports to be a list of employees of the Ministry of the Interior who worked, in April, at the Vraca school. And we see number 9. That's your name, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you do at the Vraca school in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This was the time when the Serbian part of the special police of Bosnia-Herzegovina entered the school at Vraca. And since I was the only doctor who lived in the area, I was called up to work in the medical unit in the school and the police school. And I complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's a handwritten word after your name on the list that's been translated into English as "left." Does that mean you had departed and were not there in April, or can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked there under a month at the Vraca clinic and then at the invitation of the president of the Presidency of the SFRY, Branko Kostic, I was supposed to go to Belgrade for a meeting. And I left the Vraca school and the people who were preparing the pay list for the month. They stated there that I had left, and somebody signed for me and took my salary actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't recognise the signature next to your name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's in handwriting. Somebody wrote Djokanovic in the Cyrillic script, but it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- you are aware that the Vraca school was taken over by the Serb police on or around the 6th of April 1992; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Well, I lived in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you yourself, were you actually at the school on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you go to Vraca school later in April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Two to three days after the Serbian police came into the Vraca school, I was invited or summoned by Spiric and Lubura. They had worked at the school earlier, and they knew me. They knew that I lived in the neighbourhood. They knew I was a doctor. So they invited me to come and help them with establishing a medical unit there. And I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Spiric is the -- was the principal or the head of the school at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Spiric was a professor of physical education earlier at the school -- a teacher of physical education. And earlier on, he had been a gymnast. So that's how I knew him from previously. I don't know that he was ever the principal of that school, but I do see here that it says deputy chief of that centre, which is something that I didn't know of then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see number 8 on the list is a person named Mladen Mandic who is listed at the school principal; did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did know Mandic, not too well. I knew his elder brother Momo better. But when I came to this medical unit, I knew that he was the head of the centre, the chief of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came back to Vraca a few days after the take-over, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question. What do you mean when I came back to Vraca?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you came to Vraca a few days after the take-over, how long did you remain there? Was it a matter of hours, days, weeks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I actually live at Vraca. And this school is in the immediate vicinity of the place where I live. So on a daily basis, after I actually complied with that summons, I went and did my work at the medical unit every single day until I left for Belgrade. I can't recall exactly the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know, was it in April or May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it couldn't have been after the 5th of May. And I think that I was still working on that day, on the 5th of May, and that I left, I flew out of Lukavica by helicopter because I know that because on that night my parents were seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that time that you had been working at Vraca in April, who did you see there from the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Other than the people mentioned here, the people who were in my immediate surroundings at the police academy were, I saw, for instance, Karisik regularly. I had known him also for a number of years because he was an ex-athlete as well. Also another athlete Repija. I also knew Mr. Stanisic as a former athlete. And, of course, I knew that at this time he was the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did any high-ranking political members of SDS come to Vraca during the time you were there in April and early May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, Mr. Karadzic came to the school. He was accompanied by the newly appointed minister of defence, Mr. Subotic. On this occasion, we had a chat and we had lunch together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall anything that was discussed at that lunch with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Karadzic did not know where I was in those days because we had lost touch some 15 to 30 days earlier. He didn't know that I was at the school in Vraca, that's what we talked about. And I told him that I was to go to Belgrade. And then he told me that once I returned, it would be a good idea for me it to come to Pale. And then, after lunch, we sat with the school principal in his office, there were a number of people there, and we had an informal talk where we remained there for some 30 minutes to an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the current security situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The people there were interested in the Serbian side cutting the city in two. In other words, to divide the city from Vraca towards Skenderija by the football pitch at Kosevo. And I think somebody mentioned this to Mr. Karadzic, I can't recall who it was, and Karadzic replied that he could not issue an order to that effect; that is something that would have to be decided by the council for national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall who else was present during that discussion? Mr. Karadzic, I think you mentioned the principal, Mr. Mladen Mandic. Who else was present, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think Karisik was there and Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when you left Vraca in early May, where did you go and what did you do for the next five or six weeks up until about mid-June, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Belgrade, I was informed that the Presidency of Yugoslavia where I had had an office since late December 1991, because I was the president of the coordinating body of the convention of Yugoslavia, so my administration was in the cabinet of the member of the Presidency of the SFRY from the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Dragica Cortan was there as a secretary. She worked there. She was the chief of my administration. And they advised me that I had had a number of calls from foreign embassies who wanted to talk to me about the possibility of preserving the integrity of Yugoslavia and what activities I could take part in in order to preserve the continuity of Yugoslavia. So, at this time, I visited a number of embassies. And I had discussions with a number of people from the administration of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Belgrade and returned to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in early June of that same year, Professor Koljevic managed to fine find me in Belgrade. He -- we had a meeting; we had a conversation. He told me that it was the desire of the people at Pale to have me back there. And then we left Belgrade; we flew out in a helicopter to Pale. But I requested that before we went to Pale, we should meet with Branko Kostic, the then president, Slobodan Milosevic, and the patriarch Pavle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you said Professor Koljevic told you that it was the desire of people at Pale to have you come back, did he refer to anybody specifically? And, if not, who did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is a bit difficult, now, to recall every detail. But Karadzic had already mentioned when he was at the school in Vraca that he would have wanted me to go there, so Professor Koljevic actually said that he was conveying this wish on behalf of Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you get to Pale, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I came to Pale on the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you do once you got there? How did you get engaged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The same afternoon, I spoke to Dr. Karadzic about the situation in Pale, about the problems facing the Presidency members. I acquainted myself about the most recent decision by the Presidency about the forming of the War Presidency in the municipalities. Karadzic explained that they made that decision, that it was published in the official bulletin; but they didn't have any return information, and he believed that that decision had not really been implemented in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you given a job or a title in the summer of 1992? And if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: When Karadzic explained that they were having problems with communication with the local leaderships or, rather, the Crisis Staffs, I studied their decision about the forming of the wartime presidencies, War Presidencies, and I saw what the negative aspects of it were. And then I made a decision about the forming of military commands in the localities. And the difference was that the republican commissioner should go into the field to form the war commission and to return -- and that body was supposed to restore to power the local deputies, the civilian authorities, which were elected in the last elections, and possibility elect a new president of the Executive Board in that municipality. Karadzic immediately agreed with this proposal of mine. And, at one point, we did have a difference of opinion. I wanted the commissioner to have free reign as far as the forming of the municipal commission was, but Karadzic wanted to do it according to a formula that the commissioner should -- the body should comprise five persons, the deputy, the president, the member of the SDS party, somebody from the prominent businessman in the community, and someone who was just a citizen from that municipality. I accepted that as a compromised solution because I could see that there was a possibility to appoint two persons that I could influence on. And the commissioner possibly could have some freedom to apply creativity in choosing their staff. And then we thought, Well, let's go out to the field and see if we can actually implement this. And then, on the same day, we did the certificate on my establishment as the republican commissioner. We looked at the way we would do things and the decision, and then we decided on the first municipality where would we be able to put this actually into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who named you the republican war commissioner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The appointment was signed by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to explain or distinguish a little bit for us. We've heard some evidence about Crisis Staffs. You were aware of what the Crisis Staffs were and generally how they worked in the Republika Srpska in April and May? You had some knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In all municipalities, not just of the Serbian republic, but I think the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, some sort of Crisis Staffs were formed. The Crisis Staffs in that area were not something that was new in that period. The Crisis Staff in that area were inherited from the previous regime. If there was some sort of natural disaster or any problem, then a given territory would form a Crisis Staff that would be dealing with such problems. So in the area of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Crisis Staffs were formed, and they comprised people from the local leadership. Of course, I don't know who those people were precisely, their structure in the municipality, but I know that all municipalities did have a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to the war in 1992, Crisis Staffs -- tell me if I am correct, Crisis Staffs had generally been for sort of ad hoc situations like a natural disaster, a flood, a fire, something short term; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But during the war, the Crisis Staffs that were created actually existed much longer term, for four months, and basically took over the job of the Municipal Assemblies and running the business in the municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: They were the absolute power in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what was the difference between Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies, if there was any?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no difference in essence, and I told Dr. Karadzic this right away. You're not going to get anything by renaming the people from the Crisis Staff into the War Presidency. They can change the sign on their offices from the Crisis Staffs, they can become the War Presidencies, but they will still be the same people that you are having these problems with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you give us a general idea of what kinds of problems were being had with these members of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had complained in previous conversation that didn't have communications with offices in the field, that the decision was not implemented about the Crisis Staff. And the Crisis Staff had perhaps changed their names to War Presidencies, but they had not established contact with him. And they didn't show any desire to become a part of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so what was the idea behind war commissions, how were these going to address the problem you described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to practically drive away the members of the Crisis Staffs, to put it in a figurative way, for them to discontinue with their functions completely. For the republican commissioner to come to a point, a municipal commissioner, and for those four people with the republican commissioner, they were to find deputies as soon as possible in the municipality to assemble them, organise them, and to constitute or establish a Municipal Assembly. And to elect a new president of the municipality or to abolish or confirm the mandate to the previous one. But, in any case, we wanted to have people in the field with a first and last name who would be responsible for the situation in the field. And, of course, those same people would be then in communication with the Presidency in Pale, the government in Pale; and the whole system, in that way, would begin to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Weren't most of these people who were members of the Crisis Staffs SDS members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no other political organisations in the field who could cover such a large number of municipalities, like the SDS could perhaps in a smaller number of municipalities. There were people from other political parties in those Crisis Staffs. At this point in time, I'm just thinking of some Herzegovina municipality where people came from the Serbian Renewal Movement and were perhaps members of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is the Serbian Renewal Movement associated -- well, with whom was the Serbian Renewal Movement associated at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian Renewal Movement had a parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a deputy who was Spremo from Nevesinje. And it was in no -- he was in no way different from a deputy from the Serbian Democratic Party. He was simply a part of that entire parliamentary team in the Serbian parliament of the Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me have you take a look at 65 ter document number 1705. This is dated the 13th of June, 1992, and purports to be a notice, I guess, that you as a republican commissioner have formed a war commission for Zvornik municipality. Can you tell us about this document? It's signed by you. How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted after talking with the people in the leadership in Zvornik. I signed this document. This is the only municipality where my signature is only -- the only one on that proposal. And the people who were supposed to sign that practically didn't dare sign it because the uncontested boss in Zvornik at the time, Branko Grujic, actually did not figure and did not appear on that list, and that's why they didn't dare to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did it come about that you established this war commission without including Mr. Grujic? Can you tell us why you did that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The very first day when I came to Zvornik, I could see that Brano Grujic was not a person willing to cooperate. He was a very exclusive, vain man as far as organisation was concerned, and he wanted to preserve the existing situation in Zvornik. He wanted to continue to manage the municipality, the municipal administration. It wasn't important to him whether it was called the Crisis Staff, the provisional government, the commissioner's office, or the Wartime Presidency; he just wanted to stay in control. Another thing that I didn't like was that he didn't understand what was happening in Zvornik. He didn't want to perhaps under what was going on in Zvornik, which is what I warned him about. It's about an empty municipality or small town or territory that had been emptied - I don't know how many Muslims had remained at that point - and I had warned Grujic that they shouldn't be messing around with things like that, that one day when the war is over - because these people were people who were known, their first and last names were known - they could be charged with war crimes and genocide. It was a well intentioned warning at that time, and I had the impression that that's how they took it at the time. However, Brano Grujic happened to have a different position or different view at the time about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me have you elaborate a little bit on that. Were you familiar with Zvornik before this June 13th occasion when you went to form the war commission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a young doctor, I used to work in Zvornik. I worked there for two years. I knew the municipality very well. I worked in the town and in the outlying clinics as well. I knew a lot of people personally. And then in August 1991, wishing to protect the town where I had worked as a doctor to protect it from the war, I wanted to stop -- actually, I wanted to have a consensus in the municipality between the local Serbs and Muslims and Bosniaks, and I organised a round table where I invited Radovan Karadzic and Adil Zulfikarpasic as guests. So other than my work as a doctor in 1991, I was also politically engaged in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this visit to Zvornik around the 13th of June, 1992, what did you see and what did you learn about the situation, and what had been going on up until that date, since the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon entering Zvornik - and you enter Zvornik by a road that is located between the Drina River and the town itself, and then there is a kind of overpass and that is actually an old iron bridge erected during the time of kink Alexander Karadjordjevic, and I saw people crossing that bridge as I was going in, the bridge that is linking Zvornik and Mali Zvornik. And I have this image, a lasting image in my mind, of people, old people, specially an old woman, elderly woman in Muslim "dimije" pants. And it was very clear that this was actually a group of Muslims that was leaving Zvornik and going to Mali Zvornik that I saw. In speaking with people from Zvornik that afternoon, I asked them, Why are there old people leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were you told?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: They said then that people were leaving Zvornik because they were afraid of war and there were even buses provided for those who wanted to leave Zvornik. And then I said, Why are old people going? Old people are not afraid of death and they are not afraid of war. And then I was told that there were paramilitary groups which were harassing the population and that were practically mistreating those people from the municipal leadership. And, individually, some of those people told me, for example, Jovo Ivanovic said that he had been slapped by Arkan. Brano Grujic said that members of the Yellow Wasps had locked him up in the cellar of the municipal building. So that afternoon, I was thinking that these were people who were not bad, but they didn't know how to resolve this problem in Zvornik. And I left Zvornik that afternoon to go to the next municipality, Bratunac, however I wanted to rest a little bit in Mali Zvornik. And I noticed a man in a restaurant, a Serb actually, on the road from the municipal building. I met a local radio journalist who writes for the local paper in Sabac, and she asked me why I was in Zvornik, and I explained this to her. And then, an hour after that, I crossed into Mali Zvornik, and I went to a restaurant. And then I saw that journalist and a man whom I had registered in a group in Zvornik when I entered. When I came to Zvornik, I entered the municipal building, I entered the office of the president of the Executive Board, and then in that conference room, small conference room - there was some 15 people who were sitting there at a meeting - I entered the meeting, and I told them why I was there. They quickly finished up the meeting. I knew most of those people. I knew their faces, but I didn't know one of those men. And then I saw that man again in Mali Zvornik with this journalist, and I heard some sentences. I could see that they were analysing my story, what this journalist, I think her name was Zorica was writing down, so this made me suspicious. And that afternoon I decided not to go to Bratunac. I stayed in Zvornik. I spent the night. The next day I asked to see this deputy Jovo Mijatovic and Jovo Ivanovic, both of them from the SDS, and asked them, Who is this man? They told me that that was Marko Pavlovic, that he was the secretary of the Secretariat for national Defence on the eve of the war and that he was practically doing the same job in the Crisis Staff. That he was very close to Brano Grujic. That he actually is not from that area at all, but from somewhere in Vojvodina, from Kikinda, or Zrenjanin and that they believe that this wasn't his real name either. So this actually made me even more decisive to resolve this Zvornik in an adequate way. And then on that day I said, Can you please draft a proposal for me by tomorrow of the -- for the municipal commissioner's office, and you can -- the two of you can be in there. I will be the third person. Radislav Peric, the director of Radio Zvornik will be the fourth person. And just find some fourth [as interpreted] person from the municipality for me. Jovo Ivanovic proposed Tomislav Jasic [phoen]. This man was the secretary of the housing office. He was a very competent person. They brought him to me during the day to talk to him, and he made a very positive impression on me. And I said, All right. Prepare that for tomorrow. And then the next day the list was finished. However, nobody there dared to sign that, to participate, and I said, All right. Well I will just finish this up. And that is how this proposal for the municipal commissioner's office for the Zvornik municipality came about. After that, I went to Bratunac. And then I went to Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You went to Bratunac, Skelani, did you also go to Sekovici and Glasenica [sic], to those four locations for the purposes of forming war commissions in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Vlasenica, Sekovici, Zvornik, and Bratunac from Pale. I didn't know, then, that there was a the Serbian municipality of Skelani at that time. The first municipality that I passed on the way from Pale was Vlasenica. I didn't find anyone in the municipal building there. But in the police building, I met Mr. Djuric, Mane Djuric, I think that he was the chief of police in Vlasenica at the time, and I explained to him why I had arrived at Vlasenica. And I told him to prepare the municipal commissioner's office for me, on my way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, Doctor. I'm running short on time, so I'm going to have to speed up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate, as part of the 92 ter package, the documents 65 ter number 1706 reflects the decision for forming a war commission in Vlasenica; 1707 for Bratunac; and 10152 for Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, those decisions for those municipalities contain not only their signature, but the signature of one of the local representatives. I think, for example, Bratunac, I think it's Mr. Deronjic. And I think you've explained to us the reason that yours is the only signature in Zvornik is because of the concerns the others had about Mr. Grujic being left off; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know people in other municipalities, so I didn't have any proposals of my own. I didn't have any indications that some things were changed. I simply accepted the president of the municipal Assembly, the deputy, somebody from the business community, and a citizen. That formula was something that I worked on on that basis, and whatever they had prepared, I had taken back as proposals to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you next 65 ter number 2632. This is a document dated the 17th of June, 1992. You've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you recognise the signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Dr. Karadzic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this decision is based on a review and a report from you, Dr. Karadzic confirms the appointment of the members of the war commission for Zvornik. And if we look at the five names there, there's a difference between this document and 65 ter 1705 that we looked at before in that number 3 here is Branislav Grujic. And the name of Mr. Ivanovic who was originally proposed by you is not there. Can you explain how and why that happened? Did you have any discussion with Dr. Karadzic about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from Bratunac, I passed through Zvornik again and I met Radislav Peric, the person who was the head of the radio station and he was the first one to say that Brano Grujic, when he saw that he was not on the list, simply went nuts. And then when I came to Pale, yes, I told Peric then that I would be in Pale in a couple of hours and that somebody can call me, either him or Mijatovic or Jovo Ivanovic and then we can see what this is about. And then one or the other or perhaps both of them called and they told me what was happening with Grujic, that they can not resolve that in any way, and I then conveyed this to Dr. Karadzic and then he put Grujic on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In spite of your reservations about Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I told Dr. Karadzic and the other members of the Presidency very clearly what I had encountered in Zvornik; what I saw, who I talked with, which people I saw and what kind of people they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think that's detailed in your prior testimony in the Krajisnik case, and the Judges will have that to read. Because of the shortness of time, let me skip ahead and show you document 65 ter number 3085. While that's coming up, I will tell you this is about a meeting on the 1st of July, 1992, of the Zvornik Serb municipality war commission. You recognise the signatures on this one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are conclusions from the meetings of the war commission in Zvornik and the conclusions from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And whose signatures are those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's my signature on the right, and the signature of Jovo Mijatovic who was a deputy, and a person who was shortly before the war the president of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I forgot to tender 2632, the 17 June document signed by Dr. Karadzic. I forgot that that was not part of the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would also now like to tender 3085 which we've just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, likewise admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 02632 shall be given Exhibit P00398. While 65 ter number 03085 shall be given Exhibit P00399. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At this meeting in this document, I see item number 2 says: "Due to the specific situation, the position of Zvornik Serb municipality and the lack of staff, we are unable to resolve the following matter: The SJB chief. The war commissions requesting help from the Ministry of Interior for the permanent solution of this staffing problem." What was the nature of the problem about the SJB chief in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I obtained information about the man who was in that post, Vasilic was his last name, and I had a very negative impression of him. He was a man who was, in fact, the follower of Brano Grujic. He just stumbled into the police force by some chance, and he was totally disinterested in resolving the problems in Zvornik. In view of fact that they really did not have a professional police officer in Zvornik, the only solution to this problem could be sought from Pale, so that then we could send the competent individual to be the chief of police in Zvornik. And according to my vision, this man was supposed to get a snap-shot of Zvornik so that we have a clear picture of what was going on in Zvornik and what was going on in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what other high-ranking persons, if any, attended this meeting in Zvornik, persons at your rank or higher?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the meeting of the 1st of July, or do you mean the meeting of the day before?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, we had a meeting of the republican commission with the members of the municipal commission. I chaired this meeting, and it was attended by these other four individuals that we have mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the day before, what meeting was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The day before, there was a meeting in Zvornik of all the commissioners from the region. In other words, four commissioners from Skelani, four from Bratunac, four from Vlasenica, four from Sekovici; and this meeting was attending by Dr. Karadzic, myself and Mr. Mandic. So this was the republican delegation. And, of course, this meeting was also attended by a man who should not have been there, this man called Pavlovic, Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did he come to be in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as the meeting was held in Zvornik, he was probably taken there by Brano Grujic and this man, this Marko Pavlovic, if I can use the word, tried to mine or undermine the meeting. And Karadzic had to go back to Pale and Mandic because of a shortage of time, and we were supposed to use that time for Dr. Karadzic and me and Mr. Mandic being acquainted with the situation in the field, and a lot of this time was actually spent on this Pavlovic individual. So that when I saw what was -- how we were headed, I actually began to yell. And I asked him Well, what are you talking about, man? Do you know what this meeting is supposed to be about? So in any case, this meeting was practically without any serious constructive results. The only purpose of the meeting was really that the leaders of Republika Srpska came to meet with the members of the commissions. When I saw what happened on that day, I actually called the meeting on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said Mr. Mandic was at this meeting along with Dr. Karadzic. Which Mandic are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mladic. Mladic. General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. After this meeting, when you returned to Pale, did you have any discussions with anybody in the Ministry of the Interior about the problem with the SJB chief in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, when we signed these conclusions, I sent that paper by fax to the Presidency to Dr. Karadzic, and when I returned to Pale a day or two later, I went with a member of the Presidency, Mr. Koljevic, to Jahorina to visit the minister of the interior, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you go alone or with someone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic and I went together. And Dr. Karadzic knew of the meeting. We informed him the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you meet with him that day, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Dr. Koljevic and I went to Kosuta, that's a hotel on Mount Jahorina, where part of the police of Republika Srpska was quartered, and Mr. Stanisic had his office there. We found him in his office, and we talked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can we have the precise date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doctor, can you help us? Do you know approximately what the precise dated was? How long after that 1 July meeting in Zvornik that we've seen in Exhibit 399 was it? Was it a matter of days, a week? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting could have been the 3rd, the 4th, or the 5th of July. It couldn't have been on the 2nd, but it could have been one of these three other days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this meeting, what was said? What did you say to Mico Stanisic and what did he respond, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I informed Mr. Stanisic on the problems in Zvornik, and I also told him what the conclusion was of the municipal commission, at least as far as the aspect that was of interest to him, the appointment of the chief of police in Zvornik. Koljevic pointed out that Zvornik had especially a problem, this special problem and -- the war crimes problem that they would have, and he asked Stanisic to hear me out. Mico Stanisic listened very carefully to what I had to say. He heard me mentioning the paramilitary units. And he said that Djokanovic, he said, he confirmed, he said, Yes, Djokanovic, we have big problems with paramilitary forces, and I've already sent a dispatch to the federal secretary of the interior in Belgrade because these men actually came from there and crossed over into Republika Srpska. As for the other matter, the appointment of the chief of police, he said that there wouldn't be a problem with that, because the shortage of staff was also felt in Pale, there wasn't a sufficient number of men, but that they would try, in any case, to resolve this matter. And my impression from that meeting was that he was very interested in resolving this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was done, if anything, in Zvornik after that meeting regarding replacing the chief, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was still committed to having this meeting, convening this meeting in Zvornik so that these people could return there in mid-August, and I wanted the president of the municipality -- Municipal Assembly to be elected. I learned that, in the meantime, the chief of the police was appointed, in other words, the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska had followed through on our earlier request. I didn't have occasion in those days to meet with Mr. Stanisic and discuss this, but later, in 1994, when we were both in the government, we discussed this because this war crimes issue was something that was really dogging the Republika Srpska through the end of the war. And then I met with Mico Stanisic in a restaurant, I think the name was Tron, and he said that he had continuously implemented measures in order to resolve this problem of Zvornik and appoint the chief and also the special police commissioner. However, I wasn't happy with all this because there was no accompanying policy following in the steps of this action. There were no preparations for police action, so that it appeared or practically turned out that the police intervened in Zvornik when a member of the Yellow Wasps actually stopped, at a check-point, a member of the Assembly, Mr. Ostojic, who was the second man in the SDS before the war, he stopped him at the check-point - and this is what I also said in my previous testimony - he actually stopped this man and made him to eat grass. I think a few days later a meeting was held of the Republika Srpska Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That Ostojic, is that Velibor Ostojic, who was the minister of information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is Velibor Ostojic, the minister of information in the first government of Republika Srpska and also the pre-war president of the executive board of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversation with him about that event with the Yellow Wasp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was an interesting story. Everyone knew of it at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'm almost out of time. Let me ask you a couple of more questions. In November of 1992 and on into 1993, did you hold a ministerial post in the government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1993, I was appointed as minister of veterans affairs, and later on, Mr. Djeric attempted, on two occasions, unsuccessfully, to reshuffle the government. And I was supposed to be one of the ministers who would actually be a member of that reshuffled government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you attend the assembly session on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was an Assembly session in Zvornik. I was -- I attended the session, and I even spoke or addressed the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is a meeting where the resignation of Mr. Djeric was discussed, or am I thinking of an earlier one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At this session, the session adopted the resignation of Branko Djeric, that was one of the items on the agenda. I don't know how much time we have, but I will say this: We attempted, throughout that summer, to make preparations for Djeric to actually put together a cabinet so that he can be responsible for its work, and once that was practically completed, he was actually -- he actually resigned and his resignation was accepted at this Assembly session. And this is where, actually, all the dirty laundry came out in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to stop there, we are out of time for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I wanted to do was have him confirm this Assembly session that he attended and talked about and another Assembly session and move those two documents in. If I can do that first thing Monday, I have no other questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Djokanovic, we are about to take the adjournment for the weekend. You have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. We are about to take the adjournment for the weekend. Having been sworn as a witness, you cannot communicate with the lawyers from either side on this matter. And in such conversations that you may have with persons outside of the court, you cannot discuss your testimony before the Tribunal. Do you understand what I've just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we resume in this courtroom at 9.00 on Monday morning, and I wish everyone a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
